en: Majjhima Nikāya 137,
Saḷāyatanavibhaṅgasutta:
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you the analysis of the six sense bases.”
“Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Six internal sense bases are to be known; six external sense bases are to be known;
six groups of consciousness are to be known; six groups of contact are to be known; eighteen mental explorations are to be known;
thirty-six courses for beings are to be known. Therein, depending on this, abandon that. [And] the three foundations of mindfulness...”
"That which the Noble One cultivates, cultivating which the Teacher is worthy to instruct a following—
that is called the unsurpassed charioteer of persons to be tamed among those who practice yoga.
This is the summary of the *Saḷāyatanavibhaṅga*.
‘The six internal sense bases are to be understood’—thus it was said. With reference to what was this said?
‘The eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, and the mind base.’
‘The six internal sense bases are to be understood’—
this is what was said, and it was said with reference to this.
‘The six external sense bases are to be understood’—
Thus it was said. With reference to what was this said?

“The base of visible forms, the base of sounds, the base of odors, the base of tastes, the base of tangibles, and the base of mental phenomena—these six external bases are to be understood. Thus it was said. With reference to this was it said.
Thus, that which was said— "This has been said in reference to this"— namely,
"The six classes of consciousness are to be understood":
in what way was this said, and with reference to what was it said?
‘Eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness—
these six classes of consciousness are to be understood’—
this is what was said, and it was said with reference to this.
‘The six bodies of contact should be understood’—so it was said. With reference to what was this said?
‘Eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact.’
‘The six bodies of contact should be understood’—
this is what was said, and it was said with reference to this.
‘The eighteen mental explorations should be understood’—
Thus indeed it was said. With reference to what was this said?
"Having seen a form with the eye, one dwells upon a form that is a basis for joy, one dwells upon a form that is a basis for grief, and one dwells upon a form that is a basis for equanimity.
Having heard a sound with the ear... [and so on]."
Having smelled an odor with the nose...
having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
having touched a tangible object with the body...

‘Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one explores a phenomenon that is a basis for joy, one explores a phenomenon that is a basis for grief, and one explores a phenomenon that is a basis for equanimity.
Thus, there are six explorations of joy, six explorations of grief, and six explorations of equanimity; these eighteen mental explorations are to be understood.
This is what was said, and it was said with reference to this.”
‘Thirty-six steps of being should be understood’—so it was said.
With reference to what was this said?

There are six kinds of joy based on the household life, six kinds of joy based on renunciation; six kinds of grief based on the household life, six kinds of grief based on renunciation; six kinds of equanimity based on the household life, and six kinds of equanimity based on renunciation.
In this context, what are the six kinds of worldly joy based on the household life?

It is the joy arising from contemplating the acquisition—or having previously acquired—forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, and charming, associated with worldly material gain;
or [the joy arising from] those forms that have passed away, ceased, and disappeared.
Joy arises in one who recollects what has changed.
Such joy as this is called joy based on the household life.
[The same applies to] sounds cognizable by the ear...
Of odors cognizable by the nose...
of flavors cognizable by the tongue...
of tangibles cognizable by the body...
Regarding mental phenomena that are desirable, lovely, and agreeable to the mind...
[and so on] ...there arises gladness. Such gladness as this is called worldly gladness.
These are the six types of worldly gladness.
In this regard, what are the six kinds of joy based on renunciation?

Having understood the impermanence of forms themselves—their change, fading away, and cessation—one understands it as it truly is with right wisdom: “Both formerly and now, all these forms are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change. This is how it is.
When one sees [this], joy arises.
Such joy as this is called joy based on renunciation.
It is the same with respect to sounds...
But as for odors...
as for tastes...
as for tangibles...
But when one has understood the impermanence of phenomena, their change, fading away, and cessation,
and sees them as they really are with correct wisdom, thinking: "Both formerly and now, all these phenomena are impermanent, suffering,
and subject to change," then gladness arises.
Whatever kind of mental joy there is of such a nature, this is called joy based on renunciation (*nekkhammasita*).
These are the six kinds of joy based on renunciation.
In that regard, what are the six kinds of grief based on the household life (*gehasita*)?
Of forms cognizable by the eye … [and so on] … of sounds cognizable by the ear …
Of odors cognizable by the nose...
of flavors cognizable by the tongue...
of tangibles cognizable by the body...
Sorrow arises when one regards the non-attainment of mental phenomena that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, and connected with worldly gain,
either as a present non-attainment, or by recollecting what was previously unobtained, past, ceased, and changed.
Whatever grief of such a kind there is, this is called grief based on the household life.
These are the six kinds of grief based on the household life.
In that regard, what are the six kinds of grief based on renunciation?
But having understood the impermanence of forms, their change, fading away, and cessation,
and having seen this as it really is with correct wisdom thus: "Both formerly and now, all these forms are impermanent, suffering,
and subject to change," one directs one's longing toward the unsurpassed liberations:
‘When indeed shall I enter and dwell in that sphere which the Noble Ones now enter and dwell in?’—
for one who thus arouses longing for the unsurpassed liberations, there arises grief conditioned by that longing.
Such grief as this is called grief based on renunciation.
But as for sounds...
[and so on] ...as for odors...
[and so on] ...as for flavors... [and so on] ...
Having understood the impermanence of tangibles...

and of mental phenomena, as well as their change, fading away, and cessation, one understands this as it really is with right wisdom: "Both formerly and now, all these phenomena are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change."
Having seen this, he conceives a longing for the unsurpassed liberations, thinking:
"When indeed shall I enter and dwell in that sphere which the Noble Ones now enter and dwell in?
As he thus conceives a longing for the unsurpassed liberations, sorrow arises conditioned by that longing.
Whatever grief of such a kind as this is called grief based on renunciation.
These are the six kinds of grief based on renunciation.
In this context, what are the six kinds of equanimity based on the household life?
When a fool, a deluded worldling—unconquered, unconqueror of the ripening of kamma, not seeing danger, and unlearned—sees a form with the eye, equanimity arises.
Such equanimity does not transcend the form;
therefore, that equanimity is called "based on the household life."
Having heard a sound with the ear...
having smelled an odor with the nose...
having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
Having touched a tangible object with the body...

having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, equanimity arises in the fool, the deluded worldling, who has not reached the goal, who has not conquered the ripening [of karma], who does not see the danger, and who is an unlearned worldling.
Such equanimity as this does not transcend the phenomena (*dhamma*).
Therefore, that equanimity is called "based on the household life.
These are the six kinds of equanimity based on the household life.
In this context, what are the six kinds of equanimity based on renunciation?
But having understood the impermanence of forms, their change, fading away, and cessation,
one who sees this as it really is with correct wisdom— thinking, "Both formerly and now, all these forms are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change"—
in such a person equanimity arises.
Such equanimity as this transcends form;
therefore, that equanimity is called "based on renunciation.
But as for sounds...
But as for odors...
as for tastes...
as for tangibles...
But having understood the impermanence of phenomena, their change, fading away, and cessation,
equanimity arises in one who sees this as it really is with right wisdom: "Both formerly and now, all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change."
Whatever equanimity such as this exists, it transcends [mere] phenomena;
therefore, that equanimity is called "based on renunciation.
These are the six types of equanimity based on renunciation.
‘Thirty-six steps of the noble ones are to be understood’—
this is said with reference to this. ‘In this regard, relying on this, abandon that’— this is said with reference to this.
Thus indeed it was said. With reference to what was this said?
Here, monks, by relying upon and depending upon those six kinds of joy based on renunciation, you should abandon and transcend those six kinds of joy based on the household life.
In this way, there is their abandonment; in this way, there is their transcendence.
In this regard, monks, by relying upon and drawing from those six kinds of grief based on renunciation, you should abandon and transcend those six kinds of grief based on the household life.
In this way, there is their abandonment; in this way, there is their transcendence.

In this regard, monks, by relying upon and drawing from those six kinds of equanimity based on renunciation, you should abandon and transcend those six kinds of equanimity based on the household life.
In this way their abandoning occurs; in this way their surmounting occurs.
In this regard, monks, by relying upon and depending upon those six kinds of joy based on renunciation, abandon those six kinds of grief based on renunciation; surmount them.
In this way their abandoning occurs; in this way their surmounting occurs.
In this regard, monks, by relying upon and depending on those six kinds of equanimity based on renunciation, you should abandon those six kinds of joy based on renunciation;
you should transcend them. In this way their abandonment occurs, and in this way their transcendence occurs.
There is, monks, equanimity that is diversified and based on diversity; there is equanimity that is unified and based on unity.
And what, monks, is equanimity that is diversified and based on diversity?
There is, monks, equanimity regarding forms; there is equanimity regarding sounds; there is equanimity regarding odors; there is equanimity regarding tastes;
there is equanimity regarding tangibles—this, monks, is equanimity that is diversified and based on diversity.
And what, monks, is equanimity that is unified and based on unity?

There is, monks, equanimity dependent on the base of infinite space; there is equanimity dependent on the base of infinite consciousness; there is equanimity dependent on the base of nothingness; there is equanimity dependent on the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—this, monks, is equanimity that is unified and based on unity.
In this regard, monks, relying upon and depending on that equanimity which is unified and based on unity, abandon and transcend that equanimity which is diversified and based on diversity.
In this way, there is its abandonment; in this way, there is its transcendence.
Relying upon and depending on non-identification, monks, abandon and transcend that equanimity which is unified and based on unity.
In this way its abandonment occurs; in this way its transcendence occurs.
"In that regard, 'Relying on this, abandon that'"—this was said with reference to this.
‘There are three foundations of mindfulness that the noble one cultivates, by cultivating which the noble one is worthy to instruct a group’—
so it was said. With reference to what was this said?
In this case, monks, a teacher teaches the Dhamma to his disciples out of compassion and seeking their welfare, out of compassion:
“This is for your benefit; this is for your happiness.
Yet his disciples do not wish to hear, they do not lend an ear, they do not apply their minds to understand, and they proceed in opposition to the Teacher’s instruction.
In that regard, monks, the Tathāgata is neither displeased, nor does he experience displeasure; he dwells uncorrupted, mindful and clearly comprehending.
This, monks, is the first foundation of mindfulness which the Noble One cultivates, by cultivating which the Teacher is worthy to instruct a community.
Furthermore, monks, out of compassion and seeking their welfare, the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to his disciples, having taken compassion upon himself:
‘This is for your welfare; this is for your happiness.
Yet some of his disciples do not wish to hear, do not lend an ear, do not apply their minds to understand, and they proceed in defiance of the Teacher’s instruction;
while other disciples wish to hear, lend an ear, apply their minds to understand, and do not proceed in defiance of the Teacher’s instruction.
In that regard, monks, the Tathāgata is neither displeased nor does he experience displeasure;
he is neither pleased nor does he experience pleasure.
Both displeasure and pleasure—
Avoiding both of these, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.
This, monks, is called the second foundation of mindfulness, which the Noble One cultivates, and cultivating which the Teacher is worthy to lead the assembly.
Furthermore, monks, the Teacher, compassionate and seeking their welfare, out of compassion, teaches the Dhamma to his disciples:
‘This is for your welfare; this is for your happiness.
His disciples listen, lend an ear, and apply their minds to understanding, and they do not act contrary to the Teacher’s instruction.
In that case, monks, the Tathāgata is pleased and experiences pleasure, and he dwells untainted, mindful and clearly comprehending.
“Monks, this is called the third foundation of mindfulness which the Noble One cultivates, cultivating which the Noble One is fit to instruct a group as a teacher.
‘There are three foundations of mindfulness which the Noble One cultivates, cultivating which the Noble One is fit to instruct a group as a teacher’—
it is with reference to this that it was said.”
‘Thus he is called the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed among those who follow the training of the yoke’—this, it was said, is so.
With reference to what was this said?
Monks, when a thoroughbred elephant is trained by an elephant-tamer, it runs in only one direction.
Either to the east, or to the west, or to the north, or to the south.
Monks, when a horse-tamer has directed a horse to be tamed, it runs in only one direction:
either to the east, or to the west, or to the north, or to the south.
“Monks, when a draft horse is urged by its trainer, it runs in only one direction:
either east, west, north, or south.
But when a man-tamer is urged by the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, he runs in all eight directions.”
One possessing form sees forms—
this is one direction;
being percipient of the formless internally, one sees forms externally— this is another direction.
This is the second direction;
he is intent upon the beautiful alone—
this is the third direction.

By completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking "space is infinite," one enters and dwells in the base of infinite space—
this is the fourth direction. By completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," one enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness.
This is the fifth direction;
having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, thinking ‘there is nothing,’ one enters and dwells in the base of nothingness—
this is the sixth direction.
By completely transcending the base of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
this is the seventh direction;
by completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling.
This is the eighth direction.
Monks, when the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has trained the person to be tamed, he ranges through these eight directions.
He is called “the unsurpassed charioteer of persons to be tamed among those who practice the art of training.”
"Thus, that which was said was said with reference to this.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Elated, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Saḷāyatanavibhaṅgasutta, the seventh, is finished.
